sections.html:
Nicholasville is the seat of Jessamine County, a home rule city south of Lexington. Nicholasville counted 28,015 people in 2010 and 31,093 in 2020. A mid-2025 estimate puts it at 33,857, up 8.8 percent from 2020. Over the half century from 1970 to 2020 the population multiplied by roughly 5.4, enough to rank the city tenth in Kentucky.

Fast growth means many commuters. The city has 12,131 households, 58.2 percent of them owner-occupied, the median home value is $226,800 and the average trip to work takes 24 minutes. The city is a logistics and commuter link between Lexington and Garrard County, and downtown sits about six miles south of the Fayette County line.

sections.h2: Costs of holding a house here
sections.html:
Median monthly housing cost is $1,410 for owners with a mortgage and $507 for owners without one. Tenants pay a median $1,147 in gross rent. Households take in a median $68,503 a year, and the typical household has 2.63 people.

In 2020, 4.8 percent of the city's 12,356 housing units stood empty. The vacancy rate was 1.2 percent for owned homes and 4.9 percent for rentals, so few owner-occupied houses sat empty. Children under 18 live in 36.5 percent of households, so family buyers matter here, and a house with usable bedrooms and a yard shows well.

Nicholasville and Jessamine County offices
OfficeWhereWhat it handles
Jessamine County Clerk101 North Main Street, (859) 885-4161, weekdays, eight in the morning until four in the afternoonRecords deeds and mortgages, collects transfer tax, keeps property records, delinquent tax desk
City Code Enforcement717 N. Main StreetComplaints, notices about tall grass, debris or unsafe structures
Planning and ZoningCity officeBuilding and electrical permit questions
Jessamine County PVACounty officeValues real estate, takes homestead and disability exemption applications

A Wilmore branch of the clerk's office keeps shorter hours than the main office.

Complaints go in through a form on the city website, and a Code Enforcement Board also hears matters. A letter about high weeds, junk in the yard or an unsafe building needs your reply first, ahead of any listing or offer.

For building and electrical permits, ask the city Planning and Zoning office which approvals your project needs, and keep copies of finished permits to hand to a buyer. Work done without a permit often stalls a financed sale, so disclose it early.

Deeds and mortgages for the city are recorded by the county clerk, who also holds the property records. The state transfer tax under KRS 142.050 falls on the seller and is paid to the clerk before the deed is accepted. The rate is 50 cents per $500 block, rounded up. Five percent of the take stays with the clerk as a collection fee, and the rest goes to the county treasurer.

Exempt transfers include a token-price deed between parent and child, a delinquent-tax sale, a foreclosure, and a deed given to avoid foreclosure.

sections.h2: Property tax and the homestead exemption
sections.html:
The Jessamine County PVA values the county's real estate, and its website lists the 2025-2026 homestead and disability exemption as $49,100. Apply through the PVA if you are 65 or older or disabled. It reduces taxable value, not the bill directly.

At closing the agent normally splits that year's bill between you and the buyer. Get the proration math ahead of time. If a bill on an inherited house has gone unpaid, ask the County Clerk's delinquent tax desk for the amount owed before you agree on a closing date.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited or vacated house
sections.html:
Heirs living far away usually want the easiest route. First settle who has authority to sign the deed, since the title company will ask. Then ask the clerk's delinquent tax desk whether any bill is open, and request the proration math so the closing statement holds no surprises. A rental the tenant has left needs a walk-through: note what must be cleaned or repaired, and keep the lease and deposit records for the buyer.

Visit the house or send someone you trust. Check the yard for tall grass and debris, since those draw a Code Enforcement notice, and an open notice has to be answered before you accept an offer. If work was done without a permit, tell every buyer up front instead of waiting for the inspection to turn it up.

1. Gather the deed, the latest tax bill, any mortgage statement and permit copies.
  2. Ask the PVA and the clerk what is owed and what exemptions apply to you.
  3. Answer any Code Enforcement notice and note any unpermitted work.
  4. Choose a route, whether an agent listing, a private sale or a cash offer, and get terms in writing.
  5. Sign a contract, then let the title company search the records and order payoffs.
  6. Sign the deed, pay the transfer tax at the clerk's counter, and have the deed recorded.

Keep the paperwork in one folder and each step goes faster. Moving for a job? Match the closing date to your start date before accepting terms, and ask the buyer to confirm it in writing. Keep every payoff letter and receipt, because a later question from the county is easier to answer with a paper trail.

After you accept an offer, the title company searches the county records and requests payoff figures. A mortgage, an unpaid tax bill or a recorded lien gets paid out of your proceeds. You sign the deed, the transfer tax is paid at the clerk's counter, and the deed is recorded. A cash buyer needs no lender appraisal, so the date can be yours to pick. A financed buyer needs time for the appraisal and loan approval.

A cash buyer attracts owners who value a firm closing date over squeezing out the last few thousand dollars. A town of 33,857 has plenty of buyers, yet a troubled house can still linger.

  • A home from an estate, with heirs far away and no appetite for fixing it up.
  • A rental whose tenant has left, leaving work to be done before it can be shown.
  • A property carrying a code complaint or work done without a permit.
  • An owner relocating on a short timeline to or from the Lexington area.

Owners relocating for a Lexington-area job often work to a fixed date, and a cash deal can close on the day you pick. Get terms in writing, compare the net with a listing once repairs and agent fees are subtracted, and ask the title company to confirm payoff figures first.

faqs.q: Which office holds a Nicholasville deed?
faqs.a: The Jessamine County Clerk at 101 North Main Street. Transfer tax is paid there before the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax on a Nicholasville sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Kentucky charges 50 cents per $500 of price under KRS 142.050, rounded up, and the clerk collects it before taking the deed.

faqs.q: What should I do about a Nicholasville code notice?
faqs.a: File a response through the Code Enforcement page or at 717 N. Main Street. Settle the notice before you pick a closing date.

faqs.q: Is there a tax break for older Jessamine County owners?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners 65 or older, or disabled, can apply through the PVA for the homestead exemption, shown as $49,100 for 2025-2026. It cuts assessed value, not the bill directly.

faqs.q: What if the property tax on an inherited Nicholasville house is unpaid?
faqs.a: Ask the County Clerk's delinquent tax desk for the amount owed before you agree on a closing date. The closing agent can then pay it from the sale proceeds.
